lessons.title: Review — three verbs that behave
lessons.gloss: review — three ordinary verbs, and what "ordinary" is about to mean

segments.text: Nothing new here. Name the three verbs of the last three chapters: to take, to ask, to help.
All three work the way you expect, and it is worth naming that out loud before the next chapter, where one does not.

In each of them, you are the one doing it. You take. You ask. You help. The person doing the verb is the person the sentence is about — exactly as in English, and exactly as in every verb you have met since hablo.
Hold on to that. It is about to be worth money.
Three origins, three very different kinds of story:
ayudar is the tidy one. Latin adiūtāre becomes English aid. Same word, two roads, and you can still hear it.
preguntar is the reshaped one — percontārī, to sound a depth with a pole. Asking as measuring how deep something goes.

tomar is the honest gap. It has no agreed origin at all. The verb Latin actually handed down for "take" was coger, and coger turned coarse across much of Latin America — so an everyday word had to come from somewhere, and nobody is sure where.
Not every word has a clean story. A course that pretended otherwise would be inventing them.

segments.instruction: the three verbs, then one sentence with each
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three verbs, then one sentence with each]

segments.prompt: Which of the three is the same word as English aid?

feedback.correct: Yes — adiutare, straight through to aid.

segments.prompt: Which of the three has no agreed etymology at all?

feedback.correct: Yes — nobody is sure. That is an honest answer, not a missing one.
feedback.incorrect: tomar. Its origin is genuinely unsettled.

segments.prompt: In all three verbs, who is the sentence about — the one doing it, or the thing done?

feedback.correct: Right. Remember that for the next chapter.
feedback.incorrect: The one doing it — which is about to stop being true.

segments.text: Which one has no settled origin? (Tomar.) In all three, who is the sentence about? (The one doing it.) Next chapter: a verb where that stops being true.
